paras: The killing of Mack Allen was the fatal shooting of a Black man, named as Mack Allen or McAllen, by Jerome Pasley and a party of neighborhood men in Grayson County, Virginia, near the North Carolina line, in mid-August 1881. Allen was accused of attempting an "outrage" on a young girl, and both accounts say he was shot dead after he fired a pistol at Pasley, who was trying to take him. Both surviving accounts give the pursuers' version, and a short Virginia news paragraph about the case was reprinted in Delaware, Washington and West Virginia.

The "Virginia News" column of the Alexandria Gazette placed the episode in Grayson County "last week" in its issue of August 24, 1881. A correspondent signing "D. I." and writing from "mouth of Wilson, Va." to the Western Sentinel of Winston, North Carolina, located it "near here, on the Carolina line," at the place of Masten Halsey, and said the dead man had claimed to come from Yadkin county. Both accounts say he was accused of an attempted "outrage" on a girl, nine years old in the correspondent's letter and ten in the Gazette, which called her "a little white girl."

According to the Sentinel's correspondent, the man came to Halsey's place, where Pasley worked, fired his pistol as he entered the yard, ordered Mrs. Halsey to get his breakfast, and went upstairs. Pasley summoned help, went upstairs and ordered him to surrender, and the man answered with a pistol shot that struck Pasley in the forearm. Pasley, whom the letter called "the officer," knocked him down while assistants grappled with him, and in the letter's wording Pasley then caught up a shotgun and fired into the man's abdomen, inflicting the wound that killed him.

The Gazette's paragraph told it differently: Allen was "followed and overtaken" by Pasley and "other men of the neighborhood," and when found he refused to be taken and fired on the party. In that version the shot hit Pasley in the wrist, and Pasley "at once raised his gun" and sent a load of buckshot through Allen, who "died instantly."
No report of an inquest, an arrest, or any official inquiry into the killing appears in the coverage.

The case reached print in two independent forms, a local letter and a brief state news item. The Western Sentinel ran the letter on August 25 under "News From the Old Dominion State," opening with "Pandemonium has suddenly broken loose hereabouts" and describing the wound in graphic detail. Its correspondent called the dead man "a spunky negro" who "fought desperately to the last, and met death with steal, voiceless indifference," and placed the story beside other local items, including a report of a hanging in Ashe County for stabbing a white girl.

The Alexandria Gazette's version, which referred to Allen as "a colored man" and stressed that the girl was white, gave the pursuers' account as fact without comment. That paragraph was reprinted under the heading "Shot Dead" in a Delaware Daily Gazette on August 25 and in the Washington Evening Star on August 27, and in the Spirit of Jefferson of Charles Town, West Virginia, on September 6, with the county garbled as "Gray county" or "Grayton county."

The two versions differ on the girl's age, on whether the man was found inside Halsey's house or overtaken after a pursuit, on whether Pasley was hit in the forearm or the wrist, and on the spelling of both names. The Sentinel letter came from a correspondent who knew Pasley and wrote from near the scene, so it gives fuller particulars, but neither account includes a version from Allen's side.

reader.title: Killing of Mack Allen
bases: Pasley and a group of neighborhood men pursued Allen to take him on an accusation of attempted outrage, and Pasley shot him dead after Allen fired a pistol at him (A1, A2).

Allen was killed by a party of three or more ('assistants', 'other men of the neighborhood') seeking to take him on a criminal accusation, but both accounts describe a shooting in an armed confrontation during an attempted capture, after Allen fired first, rather than a summary execution (A1, A2); whether Pasley had any authority to arrest is unclear, and both versions come only from the pursuers' side.

Two independent reports, a Virginia news item (A1, reprinted A3-A5) and a North Carolina paper's local correspondent (A2), agree on the core event: Pasley's party tried to take a Black man accused of an attempted outrage on a girl, he fired and wounded Pasley in the arm, and he was killed with a shotgun.

info: Mid-August 1881: 'last week' as of August 24 (A1); undated in a letter printed August 25 (A2).
At Mr. Masten Halsey's place, near Mouth of Wilson, Va., 'on the Carolina line' (A2); A1 says only that Allen was overtaken in Grayson county.
One Black man, 'Mack Allen' (A1) or 'McAllen' (A2), who claimed to have come from Yadkin county (A2).
Accused of an attempted outrage on a little girl, nine years old (A2) or a 'little white girl ten years of age' (A1).
Jerome Pasley (Pasely), who worked at Halsey's, with 'assistants' (A2) or 'other men of the neighborhood' (A1); A2 calls him 'the officer'.
